title: FlyQ 101: a fly brain in 2 bits
subtitle: How INT4 and ternary synapses simulate a real connectome, and why the ternary one over-fires
author: FlyQ

chapters.title: The fly brain is a graph
summary: A connectome is the complete wiring diagram of a brain.
FlyWire v783 has 138,639 neurons and 15,091,983 directed connections, each with a synapse count and a sign.
keyPoints: Nodes are neurons; edges are synaptic connections.
Weight = number of synapses, sign = excitatory (+) or inhibitory (−).
The median connection is only 2 synapses; the strongest is 2,405.

glossary.def: The full map of neurons and the synapses between them.
Compressed sparse row: for each neuron, a contiguous list of its outgoing edges.

lesson: A spiking simulation only needs to know, for every neuron that just fired, **who it talks to and how strongly**. That is exactly what a CSR graph stores: `indptr[u]..indptr[u+1]` is the slice of outgoing edges of neuron `u`.
Most connections are weak. That fact drives everything that follows.

quiz.q: What does edge weight mean in the FlyWire table?
options: Number of synapses, signed by neurotransmitter
quiz.explain: `Excitatory x Connectivity` is the synapse count multiplied by +1 or −1.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of edges are inhibitory?

cards.a: For every neuron, its outgoing edges stored contiguously, found through indptr.

chapters.title: Neurons in integers
summary: Each neuron is a leaky integrate-and-fire unit in Q16.16 fixed point: 1 mV = 65536.
Only 32-bit integers are needed, which is why the same maths runs on an ESP32 and in WebAssembly.
keyPoints: Rest −52 mV, threshold −45 mV, refractory 2.2 ms (22 ticks of 0.1 ms).
Synaptic input G decays by `g >> 6` every tick.
|v_rest − v| · alpha_m ≤ 38 mV · 65536 · 327 < 2³¹, so no 64-bit maths is needed.

glossary.def: Fixed point with 16 fractional bits; the integer 65536 means 1.0.
A short period after a spike when the neuron cannot fire again.

lesson: Floating point is optional. A neuron's voltage is one `int32`; one millivolt is `65536`. The leak pulls the voltage toward rest, the synaptic input pushes it up or down, and crossing −45 mV makes a spike.

quiz.q: In Q16.16, what integer represents −52 mV?

cards.q: Why is 32-bit maths enough for the leak?
cards.a: The product is at most about 8.1e8, below 2^31.

practice.text: One millivolt is {{65536}} in Q16.16, so the threshold of −45 mV is {{-2949120}}.

chapters.title: INT4 vs ternary synapses
summary: FlyQ4 stores each weight in 4 bits (−8..+7). FlyQ2 stores 2 bits: {−1, 0, +1}, so four weights fit in one byte.
Ternary decoding is a 4-entry lookup table: no sign extension, no multiply.
keyPoints: INT4 divides counts by about 2 and never rounds a real synapse to 0.
A deadzone θ drops edges with |w| < θ and shrinks the graph.
A per-polarity gain sets the size of one + or − step.

glossary.def: Edges with |count| below θ are removed from the ternary graph.
A tiny table mapping each 2-bit code to its Q16.16 post-synaptic contribution.

lesson: Four ternary weights share a byte. Code `00` means no connection, `01` is excitatory, `10` is inhibitory and `11` is unused.

quiz.q: How many ternary weights fit in one byte?
quiz.explain: Two bits each, so four per byte.

quiz.q: What does the deadzone θ do?
quiz.explain: Edges with |count| < θ are dropped, so there is less work per spike.

practice.intro: Match each 2-bit code to its meaning.
Write decode(byte, k): the ternary value (−1, 0 or +1) of the k-th (0–3) 2-bit code in a byte.
practice.hint: shift right by 2*k, mask with 3, then map 1→+1 and 2→−1

chapters.title: The ternary paradox
summary: Plain ternary (every edge → ±1) fired 1.23× as many spikes as INT4 on the full brain and ran slower.
A tick costs work proportional to spikes × out-degree, so extra spikes erased the cheaper decode.
A deadzone plus a calibrated gain brings spikes back to ~0.98× and runs 1.45× faster. Per-neuron fidelity is only moderate (ρ≈0.63).
keyPoints: Sign-only flattening weakens strong inhibitors more than the INT4 baseline does.
Edge-ops (synaptic updates) is the hardware-independent cost metric.
θ=3 with 'drive' gain keeps 33% of edges and 37% of synaptic work.
The notebook's snapshot Jaccard (≈0.79) barely changes with θ; use rate correlation too.

glossary.def: Number of synaptic updates performed; the real cost of a tick.
Scale each polarity so total excitatory and inhibitory drive match INT4 after pruning.

lesson: More spikes means more edges walked per tick, so a cheaper edge does not help if there are 30% more of them. The fix is not a faster decoder but a better quantizer.
There is no free lunch: the further you prune, the faster it runs and the less it resembles INT4's per-neuron activity.

quiz.q: Why was plain ternary slower than INT4?
options: It produced more spikes, so more edges were traversed
quiz.explain: Cost scales with spikes × out-degree; 23% more spikes outweighed the cheaper decode.
Edge-ops counts synaptic updates regardless of the machine.

cards.a: θ=3 with the drive gain: spikes ×0.98, 1.45× faster, 33% of edges.

practice.intro: Put the explanation of the paradox in order.
items: Plain ternary flattens strong inhibitory synapses to −1
Inhibition is weaker than in INT4
The network fires about 23% more spikes
Each spike walks its whole edge list
Total synaptic work rises and the run is slower

questions.q: How many bits does one ternary synapse use?
What is the real cost driver of a connectome tick?
questions.explain: Each spike walks its outgoing edges.
It removes weak edges from the ternary graph.

questions.q: Which is true of the θ=3 drive result?
options: Spikes ≈0.98× INT4 and it is 1.45× faster
questions.explain: It matches activity in total, but per-neuron correlation is only about 0.63.
